newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless rate fell to 5.1 percent in August.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless rate fell to 5.1 percent in August.

text.p: The unemployment rate dropped to 5.1 percent last month, its lowest level in more than seven years, from 5.4 percent in July amid broad-based, solid growth in jobs, the government said Friday.

In the government's first assessment of the economy's health in August, the Labour Department said 250,000 non-farm jobs were created during the month for a total of 120 million, after 228,000 were created in July.
Wall Street economists surveyed by Reuters had projected an August unemployment rate of 5.3 percent and the creation of 244,000 jobs.

The decline in the unemployment rate, which was especially steep among workers over 55 and in their early 20s, brought the jobless rate to its lowest level since March 1989, when it was 5 percent, the department said.

Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics, attributed some of the jobless rate decline to statistical distortions in assessing the seasonal movement of unemployed youth. But she said other evidence suggested a genuine job market improvement.

Financial markets had been eagerly awaiting the department's monthly report to scour it for signs of whether the economy is heating up to the point that it could fuel inflationary pressures and prompt Federal Reserve policymakers to pre-emptively raise interest rates.

Some recent economic data have indicated a modest slowing, espcially in the housing sector. But there is concern that it will not be enough to stop Fed policymakers from raising interest rates. Many economists believe the question is not whether rates will be raised but when.

"Clearly that low unemployment rate is going to scare the Fed and I think that makes a Fed rate hike more likely this month. Their concern is inflation," said David Wyss, Research Director at DRI/McGraw Hill.

Workers' average hourly earnings, which have been scrutinised more closely lately by traders for signs of wage-push pressure on prices, rose by 6 cents last month to $11.87 after falling 2 cents in July. Over the past year, hourly earnings rose 3.6 percent.

"That's quite a negative development," said Dan Seto, Senior Economist at Nikko Securities Co. International Inc. "We had been concerned that after the 0.2 percent drop last month you would get a significant bounce. That's what we've got.
"On a year-to-year basis, the earnings are up by 3.6 percent. That's clearly outpacing the perceived 3.0 percent inflation rate."

While the jobs created last month were widely spread throughout the economy, many were in local government employment, especially in education, and in services, in particular business, temporary help and computer services, the department said.
In the industrial sector, which has been showing signs of strength lately, the number of manufacturing jobs rose by 25,000 in August after falling by 27,000 in July.
The factory workweek rose by 6 minutes last month to 41.7 hours, while overtime was unchanged at 4.4 hours a week, it said.
The department's survey of households showed that the number of jobless workers fell by 467,000 last month to 6.8 million, while those with jobs rose by 171,000 to 127.1 million, the department said.
The civilian labour force, which includes employed workers and those seeking jobs, fell by 296,000 to 133.9 million, it added.
